worksheet.title: Does the Order Work?
worksheet.subtitle: Read the algorithm and check the order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can tell if an algorithm's steps are in an order that works.

parts.title: Check the order
parts.text: Read each algorithm. Does the order make sense? Circle YES if it works, or NO if a step is in the wrong place. Then tell why. A step that needs another step must come AFTER it.

parts.title: Does A work?
parts.prompt: Circle YES or NO. Tell why the order does or does not work.

blocks.label: 3. pour the cereal in the bowl

parts.title: Does B work?
parts.prompt: Circle YES or NO. Tell what is wrong with the order.

parts.title: Algorithm C — go down the slide
You try — C does not work
parts.prompt: Circle YES or NO. Then write the 3 steps of C in an order that DOES work.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: An algorithm only works if every step comes after the steps it needs. If a step is in the wrong place, the order does not work — even if all the steps are there.

teacher_guide.title: Does the Order Work?
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 5. Does the Order Work? — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students read three plans and judge whether the order works, explaining why, then rewrite a broken one. Reading a plan and deciding if the order succeeds — and fixing it — is the heart of debugging. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: cut the steps into cards so students can physically slide them into order before writing.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Read a plan aloud and ask: "does each step have what it needs?"
2. Do one together. Plan A works; Plan B does not (you cannot eat before you pour).
3. Let them try. Students judge Plan C and rewrite it so it works.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Plan A WORKS (YES): draw the circle, add rays, colour it — each step has what it needs.
Exercise 2 — Plan B does NOT work (NO): eating is first, but you must pour the cereal then the milk before you can eat; eating should be last.
Exercise 3 — Plan C does NOT work (NO). A working order: climb the ladder, sit at the top, slide down (you must sit before you slide).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: saying YES because the steps look familiar. Check each step has what it needs from earlier steps.
Make it easier: act out the broken plan so the problem is obvious.
Make it harder: ask them to explain exactly which step is too early and why.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students put step-by-step instructions in the right order to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a set of steps, change or reorder one, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child judges each plan correctly and rewrites the broken one into a working order.
